rationale: B wins because it turns the same evidence into sharper reporting assignments and says where each one breaks, especially "One retrofitted Sweetgreen, before and after the conveyor" and the warning that it "does not exist until that data does." A has two strong live angles, but "The $15 salad is now assembled by robot" smuggles in a price point and an unsupported premium-category thesis. That is the difference between strategic discipline and a good angle wearing borrowed clothes.
gaps_in_A: "The $15 salad is now assembled by robot" invents a price point the update never gave. Cute headline, bad habit.
"premium, customizable, ingredient-forward) was supposed to be the tier where automation couldn't go" is an unsupported category premise. It may be true, but this set has not earned it.
"ongoing fights around restaurant-worker protections and minimum wage" adds a broad policy backdrop without a specific live peg from the update. Either prove the peg or cut the decoration.
"meanest-editor" as the next step is the wrong handoff. The founder needs proof gathering and journalist fit, not another critique lap.
gaps_in_B: "the beat that has watched automation live mostly in pilots and demo units" is outside industry context not supplied by the update. Prove it or soften it.
"funding-mechanics" is the wrong label for the markets angle. This is public-company unit economics and profitability, not financing mechanics.

"One retrofitted Sweetgreen, before and after the conveyor" is the best trade idea, but it is not pitch-ready today. The set correctly admits it "does not exist until that data does"; keep it out of the live announcement batch.
"restaurant-tech" is a little loose as a beat label. The stronger target is restaurant operations or unit-economics trade coverage, not shiny-robot vendor coverage.
